name: The Great Schism and the conciliar resolution
plain_explanation: After Gregory XI's death, disputed elections produced two rival popes -- Urban VI in Rome and Clement VII in Avignon -- each recognized by different, largely politically-determined coalitions of states (France backed Avignon; France's enemies backed Rome). Since a legitimate pope should logically outrank any other authority, only something above both claimants -- a General Council -- could resolve the impasse. A first attempt at Pisa (1409) backfired, producing a third pope instead of resolving the dispute. The Council of Constance (1414-18) finally succeeded: it decreed popes cannot dissolve councils and must submit to them, deposed the discredited claimants, and secured the uncontested election of Martin V in 1417.
precise_definition: The nearly forty-year period (1378-1417) during which rival papal claimants, based respectively in Rome and Avignon, divided Catholic Christendom along largely national political lines, finally resolved by the Council of Constance's assertion of conciliar authority over the papacy.
why_it_mattered: It represents the most severe institutional crisis of the medieval papacy, demonstrating in practice the conciliarist theory (Marsiglio, Occam) developed in the previous chapter, even though the movement's larger ambition -- permanently subordinating the papacy to regular General Councils -- ultimately failed once the schism itself was healed.
historical_origin: Begins with the disputed 1378 election following Gregory XI's death; resolved at the Council of Constance, 1414-18.
examples: The Council of Pisa's (1409) failed attempt, which deposed both existing popes but elected a third (eventually the notorious ex-pirate John XXIII), yielding three popes instead of resolving anything
The Council of Constance's condemnation and execution of Huss despite a promised safe conduct, and its posthumous exhumation and burning of Wycliffe's bones
influence_on_later_thinkers: The subsequent Council of Basel (from 1431) was decisively defeated by Pope Eugenius IV by 1448, showing the conciliar movement's ultimate failure to permanently constrain papal authority, even as the papacy 'emerged politically triumphant, but with very greatly diminished power of inspiring moral reverence.'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: National political alignments (France vs. its enemies, Scotland vs. England) directly determined which pope different countries recognized, illustrating the schism's essentially political character.
